Part 1 asks what a claim in social science is for, why people describe the field as being in crisis, and how three very large studies measured the problem, one of which supplies the case study of the day. It ends on that case study, the paper and the claim that five analysts reanalysed, and on R running on your machine. The hands-on work comes at the end and runs into the first break, so that if your machine gives trouble you miss none of the talk.

## 1. The plan of the day

**On the slides.** The facilitator sets out the plan of the day and its two kinds of aim, what you will understand and what you will be able to do. The slides also say what you do not need: nothing to install on the day, no git, and no GitHub or OSF account. Open your workspace in your IDE while the facilitator talks, and the deck in a tab of its own.

[Open the deck](../../live/day.html){.btn .btn-outline-primary target="_blank"}

## 2. The credibility of social science

**On the slides.** Follow the talk on what social science is for, on false positives and forking paths, and on the evidence from replications and many-analysts studies. It goes on to incentives and questionable research practices, which matter far more than fraud, and to the red-card study, in which twenty-nine teams analysed one dataset, with the estimates that they returned. It then shows why 'replication' names three different operations, set out as a matrix of data against analysis with a quick check on it, and ends on the practices of open research.

## 3. SCORE {#score}

**On the slides.** The SCORE programme ran three studies, of reproducibility, robustness and replicability, and the slides give the result of each in brief. They then present the robustness study (Multi100; Aczel et al. 2026) from the position of an analyst inside it: what an analyst received, the two tasks, and how the results were put on a common scale.

To go further: [SCORE](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/score.html) on the AR4DS site.

## 4. The paper and its claim

**On the slides.** The slides present the paper of the original authors (OAs): the question that it asks, the design, the email word for word, what came back for each of the six names, and the four outcomes that were coded. They end on the claim as SCORE selected it, with its two ellipses.

## 5. The workspace and the deck

**On the slides.** The workspace, in which you work, and the deck, which shows each step and runs it in your browser, hold the same tasks and give the same numbers. The slides show what each of them offers and what the tools cannot do.

## 6. Task 1 – The setup check

**In your workspace.** Open its folder in your IDE and run `source("R/check_setup.R")` until every line prints OK. The last check fits the reference specification and prints −19.97 percentage points, a number that you meet again later. Then read the four scenarios of the warm-up in the box of Task 1 of `index.qmd`, which ask you to name the R that each of them describes, and one of the scenarios describes none of the three. If you need more time, carry on into the break.

[Open the deck at Task 1](../../live/day.html#/hands-on-1-get-yourself-running){.btn .btn-outline-primary target="_blank"} [Open the browser lab at Task 1](../../lab.qmd#task-1-setup){.btn .btn-outline-primary target="_blank"}

The deck shows the setup check and the [warm-up](../../live/day.html#/hands-on-1-the-warm-up){target="_blank"} with their output. If your installation fails, run the same cells in the deck or in the browser lab, which give the same numbers.

**By the end of the part** you can tell apart the three operations that go under the single word 'replication', you know the claim on which the day works, and you have R running in your workspace, or in the deck if your installation failed, with the 1,014 emails of the Housing data loaded.
